JP Aerospace is a volunteer-based DIY Space Program.

I've followed this project for a while. Dirigible spacecraft are a promising but overlooked area in spacecraft design. By getting something to stratospheric altitude first, one can employ longer, gentler acceleration periods using simpler and higher ISP propulsion while radically reducing vehicle mass. Spacecraft can be based on light truss structures based on modular elements with minimal streamlining--even tensegrity structures--that are more easily fabricated, mass-produced, and recycled in space than typical monocoque rocket structures. And though the notion of vast reusable manned vehicles may be a bit of a stretch, the concept would bring basic space access down to a university level. You might actually launch student-built LEO spacecraft from a campus parking lot.

Sadly, it doesn't seem that the space advocacy community has much interest in actually doing things and so DIY and open space development remains nascent. People are so belabored by preconceptions of what space activity is supposed to be that they overlook the vast assortment of things regular folks might actually participate in. If it's not promising a seat in Capt. Kirk's chair tomorrow, it's not relevant. Space enthusiasts today seem far more interested in just being a passive audience to the public spectacles of state and oligarchs, and then wonder why half a century went by with so little accomplished toward public access to space. I've been shopping around the concept for an amateur open source space program based on telerobot development for years now, and there's never any interest or feedback. Too much effort. Better to just sit around and wax poetic about 'the dream' while hoping for a free ride from Elon Musk.
